intent.asked: Set up a new project, UTP: a refined method for agents to hand you decisions in structured formats suited to the type of decision, so you review them easily instead of decoding conceptual replies. Research open-source prior art, shape it from real sessions with a focus on decisions that had to be backtracked, roundtable the concept until it holds up, and present the concept for review. Make it work with Codex and Antigravity, command line first, desktop features optional.
intent.doing: Presenting the concept and its seven open decisions. Nothing is built yet.

deferred.reason: It starts after you answer these decisions.

deferred.item: Native question dialogs, the local review page, the phone inbox and an MCP server
deferred.reason: The roundtable sequenced them after the command-line core is proven.

added.item: A private evidence corpus of 60 decision cases from your recent sessions
added.reason: It grounds the design; it stays out of the public repository.

requests.question: Which kinds of request should the first working version handle?
requests.why_now: Phase 1's size and order depend on it.

options.label: The six the evidence points to
options.consequence: By decision type, the six kinds cover 50 of the 60 evidence cases, and review batching and the evidence rules cover 6 more: choices, approvals, manual steps, clarifications, completion checks and plan assumptions, plus FYI notices. Phase 1 takes longer, but the six share one lifecycle, so each adds a schema, a template and lint rules rather than new machinery.

options.label: Choices and approvals only
options.consequence: A usable first version sooner. Manual handoffs (8 cases) and acceptance of results (5 cases) keep going through chat. Completion reports still map each goal, written as plain Markdown, and the phase 1 criteria for the deferred kinds move to phase 2.

options.label: The six plus blind judging
options.consequence: Brings the blind-ballot pages into UTP right away, but phase 1 then needs the local review page, which delays the command-line core.

recommendation.because: They are the most frequent decision types in the evidence, and they share one lifecycle. The evidence counts cases; it doesn't measure rework cost.
recommendation.preserves: The blind-ballot pages keep working as they are until phase 2.
recommendation.bolder_alternative: Option c, if you want blind judging in the first release.

evidence.claim: Decision types across the 60 cases: approach 8, approval 8, manual handoff 8, intent 7, process 7, acceptance 5, prioritization 4, batches 3, plan defaults 3, diagnosis 3, judging 2, understanding 2.

requests.level_reason: Scope of the first release is the person's call.

requests.question: Where should each project's decision log live?
requests.why_now: The first stored request needs a home, and the reviewers found that the obvious place, a folder inside the repository, splits the log across worktrees.

options.label: In your home folder, one log per project per machine
options.consequence: Every branch and worktree of a checkout shares its log automatically. Another clone of the same project on that machine shares it once you link it with one confirmation; until then it keeps its own log, and a clone that already has records keeps them as a searchable, read-only archive after linking. No commit can include the log. Agents in a restricted sandbox (Codex's default mode, for example) need a one-time setting to write to this folder; `utp setup` shows it and applies it after you confirm. Each machine keeps its own log, so a project worked on from two machines has two independent logs. Moving to a shared store later needs a migration tool, planned for phase 3.

options.label: Inside each repository, ignored by Git
options.consequence: The log sits next to the code, but each worktree gets its own copy, so agents in different worktrees don't see each other's decisions. Works in agents' default sandboxes with no setup.

options.label: Inside each repository, committed
options.consequence: Shared between machines through Git, but decisions become part of the history (a public repository would publish them) and parallel agents collide in merge conflicts. Works in agents' default sandboxes with no setup.

options.label: One central log on the home server
options.consequence: One log across every machine, but nothing works until the server is reachable and a service is running. Agents whose sandbox blocks network access can't reach it.

recommendation.because: Agents routinely work in separate worktrees here, and two reviewers flagged writes to synced copies as unsafe.
recommendation.preserves: Plain files and a command-line tool, with no service to run.
recommendation.bolder_alternative: Option d, as a later phase once the format settles.

requests.notes: With any option, UTP's own design decisions are exported, redacted, into this repository's docs/decisions folder.
requests.level_reason: Architecture choice that later data depends on.

requests.question: What should UTP be written in?
requests.why_now: The phase 1 code starts in this language.

options.label: Python, standard library only
options.consequence: Runs anywhere Python 3.11 or later exists, with nothing else to install, and reuses the ballot-server code. The terminal review uses plain numbered prompts rather than a full-screen interface.

options.label: Python with a few libraries
options.consequence: A nicer full-screen terminal review and stricter schema validation, but each machine needs a pip install first.

options.label: TypeScript on Node
options.consequence: Closer to MCP and web tooling, but a second runtime on every machine, and the existing Python review code can't be reused.

recommendation.because: Nothing to install, and it builds directly on code that already works.
recommendation.preserves: One language across the existing review tools.
recommendation.bolder_alternative: Option c, if the review page grows into a full web app.

evidence.claim: The three blind-ballot servers and the roundtable engine are Python standard-library code.

requests.level_reason: Hard to change once code exists.

requests.question: When an agent reaches work that depends on a question you haven't answered, what should it do?
requests.why_now: This sets how often you get asked and how much an agent can get done while it waits.

options.label: Use its default only for small, easy-to-undo, non-design questions
options.consequence: Agents keep moving on minor reversible choices, and each default they used shows up in your next review as 'applied by default: change?'. Design, scope, approval and acceptance questions always wait for you.

options.label: Always wait
options.consequence: No wrong turns from defaults, but agents sit idle more and ask you sooner and more often.

options.label: Use the default for any reversible clarify or choose question
options.consequence: Fastest: defaults also cover design and scope questions, as long as they are easy to undo. Approvals, acceptances, judgments and anything the agent lacks authority for still always wait. The research found your overrides clustered in design questions, so expect rework whenever a default was the wrong call.

recommendation.because: Of the 72 questions with a recommendation that you answered, you chose something else 37 times, and the research noted those overrides clustered in design questions. That small reversible choices rarely matter is a judgment, not a measured result.
recommendation.preserves: Your rule that agents decide routine things themselves.

evidence.claim: Recommended option chosen 35 of 77 times; another listed option 18; your own answer 19; dismissed 5. The research noted overrides clustered in design questions but gives no per-category counts.

requests.level_reason: Sets the asking policy the person lives with.

requests.question: Where do you want to answer UTP requests by default?
requests.why_now: Phase 1 builds the default channel first; the others arrive in the phases shown.

options.label: In the conversation
options.consequence: No new window for most questions. The agent shows lettered cards and logs your reply with a quote it checks against the session transcript. A consequential approval must name the action, unless it's a quick 'yes' right after a single card. On Antigravity, whose transcripts can't be checked, consequential approvals go to a terminal review instead. Reviews with previews open a local page once phase 2 lands.

options.label: Always on a separate review page
options.consequence: Every answer is captured directly with no agent in between, but you switch windows for every question, and the review page moves into phase 1, which makes phase 1 longer.

options.label: In the app's own question dialog
options.consequence: Familiar one-click answers, but the consequence lines must fit the dialog, what Codex offers depends on the client and mode, and one of its question tools pre-selects the first option, which the adapter has to work around, and Antigravity's command line can't answer it. It arrives in phase 2; until then you answer in the conversation as in option a. Moving the dialogs into phase 1 would add their per-platform mapping and conformance tests to phase 1.

recommendation.because: You answered 168 structured questions inside sessions; a separate window for every answer is the kind of friction that gets routed around.
recommendation.preserves: The conversation as your main surface.
recommendation.bolder_alternative: Option b, for the strongest guarantee that every answer came from you.

evidence.claim: 168 answers to agents' structured questions in recent sessions.

requests.level_reason: Sets the person's daily experience of UTP.

requests.question: UTP plans to absorb, connect to, or leave alone these existing tools. Keep or change each plan?
requests.why_now: It decides what phase 1 to 4 build and what they reuse.

items.label: Blind-ballot review pages from the design lab
items.proposal: Absorb into UTP's blind judging: phase 2, or phase 1 if you pick D1 option c
items.consequence: One maintained copy instead of three; the experiments move to UTP's page.

items.label: Phone inbox
items.proposal: Connect as an answer channel in phase 4
items.consequence: You can answer cards from the phone; its 24-hour text purge stays and UTP keeps the record.

items.label: Open-items list
items.proposal: Connect: UTP's waiting requests appear there
items.consequence: One list of what's waiting on you instead of two.

items.label: Push notifications and the morning report
items.proposal: Connect: one notification per review; notices go to the morning report

items.label: Concept and divergence register
items.proposal: Leave alone; copy its trigger, reversal and history fields

items.label: Interview-me question skill
items.proposal: Fold its rules into how UTP writes clarify cards
items.consequence: The skill's rules carry on in UTP's templates.

items.label: Brass-tacks summaries
items.proposal: Reuse as the summary layer at the top of each review
items.consequence: The three-layer shape you already know opens every review.

recommendation.because: Each plan reuses something that works and avoids a second copy.
recommendation.preserves: Every existing tool keeps working until UTP replaces or connects to it.
recommendation.bolder_alternative: Absorb the open-items list into UTP entirely.

requests.level_reason: Reversible plan; each item can change later.

requests.question: What license should the public UTP repository carry?
requests.why_now: The repository is public and has no license file yet.

options.label: MIT
options.consequence: Anyone can reuse it with attribution, the same as your other public repositories. You can change the license for later versions, but copies already released under MIT keep MIT's terms.

options.label: Apache 2.0
options.consequence: Adds an explicit patent grant and a longer text. Its grants for released versions are perpetual and irrevocable, so a later change applies to new versions only.

options.label: No license for now
options.consequence: All rights reserved: others can read it but can't legally reuse it. Easy to change later, since nothing has been granted yet.

recommendation.because: Six of your public repositories already use MIT.
recommendation.bolder_alternative: None; this is a consistency choice.

evidence.claim: LICENSE files in torc-concept-review, wsl-plus-public, brass-tacks, masq-voice, tali and weir all begin 'MIT License', and GitHub detects each one as MIT.

requests.level_reason: Outward-facing, and grants for released copies can't be withdrawn.
